Lothal: An important Harappan centre in Gujarat

Lothal is a major Harappan archaeological site in Gujarat, situated near the Bhogava River, a tributary associated with the Sabarmati system, and close to the Gulf of Khambat.

Lothal is especially important for understanding the relationship between urban planning, storage facilities, craft production and possible water-based transportation.

The upper and lower sections of Lothal

Lothal had an elevated upper section, often described as the Acropolis or Citadel, and a Lower Town containing residential and other buildings.

The settlement had substantial fortifications. However, unlike the separately walled Citadel at Mohenjodaro, Lothal's raised upper section was not independently enclosed by its own wall.

Excavations have revealed houses, streets, bathing facilities and an organised drainage system. Although many houses were constructed using mud bricks, baked bricks were used for drains.

The warehouse and its role

One of Lothal's important structures is a large building identified as a warehouse or storehouse.

Seals and clay impressions of seals were recovered from the storage-related area. Such clay impressions, called sealings, could be used to secure or identify packages of goods.

The combination of a substantial storage structure and evidence of sealed goods supports the interpretation that Lothal had facilities associated with handling or storing materials.

A bead-making workshop has also been identified in the Lower Town. Its existence provides an example of specialised productive activity within a planned urban settlement.

The large basin traditionally called a dockyard

Lothal is widely associated with a large rectangular brick-lined basin that has traditionally been identified as a dockyard.

A dockyard is a protected water area where boats or ships may be received, sheltered, loaded or unloaded.

The proposed dockyard interpretation connects the basin with Lothal's position near an ancient watercourse and the Gulf of Khambat. Such a facility could have supported the movement of goods by water.

However, the interpretation is not universally accepted. Some researchers have proposed that the basin served as a water-storage reservoir instead. The precise function of the structure remains debated.

For objective examinations, the safest distinction is between the physical structure, which is an established archaeological find, and its proposed function as a dockyard.

Lothal's dockyard identification

Lothal contains a large rectangular basin traditionally identified as a dockyard. Its function is debated, so it is more accurate to describe it as a structure interpreted as a dockyard than to treat that interpretation as conclusively established.

Kalibangan and Surkotada: Two further comparisons

Kalibangan, Rajasthan

Kalibangan had a fortified Citadel and a planned Lower Town with streets arranged in a broadly gridiron pattern. It is also associated with structures interpreted as fire altars.

Its domestic wastewater arrangements provide an important contrast with Mohenjodaro. Household drains at Kalibangan commonly discharged into soakage jars, rather than forming part of an extensive, regular network of continuous street drains.

Surkotada, Gujarat

Surkotada, in Kutch, was a much smaller Harappan settlement. Its excavated remains show a fortified Citadel associated with an adjoining residential section.

Construction included mud bricks and stone rubble. Surkotada demonstrates that substantial fortifications and the division of settlement space were not confined to the largest Harappan cities.

Comparing major sites through their distinctive architecture

SiteLocationImportant architectural association
MohenjodaroSindh, PakistanGreat Bath, extensive wells, planned drainage
HarappaPunjab, PakistanLarge brick building traditionally called a granary
DholaviraKutch, Gujarat3-part settlement, stone fortifications, reservoirs
LothalGujaratWarehouse, drainage, large basin interpreted as a dockyard
KalibanganRajasthanGridiron town, fortified sections, soakage jars
SurkotadaKutch, GujaratFortified Citadel and adjoining residential section

What remained common despite regional differences?

The Harappan settlements were not identical, but several important principles can be recognised across the civilisation.

Builders commonly organised settlement space into distinguishable sections, used durable construction materials, provided routes for movement and developed arrangements for water supply or wastewater disposal.

At the same time, individual settlements responded to different local conditions. Mohenjodaro emphasised extensive wells and connected drains; Dholavira developed reservoirs and substantial stone architecture; Lothal contained storage facilities and a large basin associated with possible water transport; Kalibangan used a different method of household wastewater disposal.

These examples show that Harappan urban planning combined shared construction practices with local variation.

Prelims focus

  • Lothal is associated with the Bhogava River and the Gulf of Khambat region.
  • Lothal had a raised upper section, a Lower Town and substantial settlement fortifications.
  • Its important structures include a warehouse and a large basin traditionally called a dockyard.
  • Kalibangan had a planned street pattern and household drainage arrangements involving soakage jars.
  • Surkotada, in Kutch, had a fortified Citadel and adjoining residential section.
  • Trap: The famous Great Bath is at Mohenjodaro, the extensive reservoir system is especially associated with Dholavira, and the large basin traditionally identified as a dockyard is at Lothal.
